name: Ayurvedic amla / bhringraj / shikakai

lead: Amla (Indian gooseberry), bhringraj (Eclipta prostrata) and shikakai (a pod used as a mild cleanser) are South Asian herbs used on hair as powders, pastes and oils. Traditional users say they cleanse, condition, strengthen and promote growth or darkening.

Amla's tannins and vitamin C underlie the antioxidant claims in laboratory work, and shikakai-type plants are said to cleanse through natural saponins. Bhringraj leaves were steeped in coconut oil as a once-popular hair oil. No clinical hair trials of these herbs were found.

paras: People mix the powders into pastes for a pre-wash hair mask, use shikakai as a gentle shampoo alternative, or apply infused oils to the scalp and hair. It is a regular routine in traditional hair care, often with the three combined. Users describe softness quickly and look of fullness over months.

The sources reviewed give no safety data for topical hair use. Wikipedia says no high-quality clinical research supports the traditional uses of bhringraj. As with any plant product, a patch test is a common precaution.

chain: Traditional herbs as oils or pastes
angle.text: Amla, bhringraj and shikakai are traditional Ayurvedic herbs used as pastes, powders and oils to cleanse and condition hair for a fuller, healthier look. They have centuries of use, and laboratory work has examined amla antioxidants; no clinical hair trials exist.

lead: Amla, bhringraj and shikakai are three plant materials from the Ayurvedic tradition of South Asia that are used in hair care, commonly as powders, pastes or infused oils. Amla is the fruit of Phyllanthus emblica (Indian gooseberry); bhringraj usually refers to Eclipta prostrata; shikakai is a pod-bearing plant used as a mild natural cleanser.

Practitioners of traditional hair care say these ingredients cleanse, condition and strengthen hair and promote growth or darkening. Wikipedia notes that Eclipta prostrata has been steeped in coconut oil as a hair oil that was popular until the 1970s and that its leaves yield a black hair dye [1], and that there is no high-quality clinical research supporting its traditional uses [1].
Laboratory work on amla has examined antioxidant properties of its extract [2][3]. No clinical trial of these herbs for hair growth was identified in the sources reviewed.
infobox: Phyllanthus emblica fruit, rich in vitamin C [4]
Eclipta prostrata; also name of a different plant, Wedelia calendulacea [1]
Traditional pod-based hair cleanser (not covered in encyclopedia sources reviewed)

paras: Phyllanthus emblica is a deciduous tree native to tropical and southern Asia, with a greenish-yellow fruit high in ascorbic acid and containing ellagitannins, flavonoids, and gallic and ellagic acids [4]. The fruit is eaten raw, pickled or candied, and is a common ingredient in Ayurveda [4]. It features in Buddhist and Hindu tradition [4].

In Hindi-speaking regions the name bhringaraj is applied to Eclipta prostrata, a daisy-family plant native to the Americas and now common worldwide as a weed, and also to a yellow-flowered species, Wedelia calendulacea [1]. Its dried whole plant appears in Southeast Asian traditional medicine, and it has been used as a hair-oil herb and as a source of black dye [1].

Shikakai is the traditional name for a pod used as a gentle cleanser. The encyclopedia entry on soapnuts (Sapindus), a related type of saponin-containing cleanser, describes the pulp being used to make soap and shampoo, with surfactant-acting saponins [5]. That entry does not mention shikakai itself.

A 2016 review of amla covers its phytochemistry, ethnomedicinal uses and proposed mechanisms [2], and an in vitro study compared antioxidant, anti-collagenase and anti-elastase activity of amla extract for anti-ageing skin applications [3]. These are laboratory or review sources and do not test hair outcomes. Wikipedia states that no high-quality clinical research supports the traditional uses of Eclipta prostrata [1].
No studies found. Laboratory research on amla antioxidant activity exists [3], but it does not address hair growth or hair quality in people.
